exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = -e^{2y-x}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2e^{2y-x} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &=- e^{2\sin t-\cos t}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= 2e^{2\sin t-\cos t}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = -\sin t, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} = \cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} &= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \\[5pt] &=- e^{2\sin t-\cos t} \cdot (-\sin t) + 2 e^{2\sin t-\cos t} \cdot \cos t \\[5pt] &=(\sin t+2\cos t)e^{2\sin t-\cos t} . \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x = x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}s} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = e^{x+2y} , \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2e^{x+2y} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= e^{s^2+2s},\\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &=2e^{s^2+2s}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}s} = 2s, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}s} = 1. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}s} & = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}s} \\[5pt] &=e^{s^2+2s}\cdot 2s + 2e^{s^2+2s} \cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= 2se^{s^2+2s}+ 2e^{s^2+2s}\\[5pt] &= 2(s+1)e^{s^2+2s}. \end{align*}

question.text: If $f(x,y)=\ln(xy^2), x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t,$ compute $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t}$ for $0 < t < \dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{y^2}{xy^2}=\dfrac 1x, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac{2xy}{xy^2}=\dfrac 2{y} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &=\dfrac 1{\cos t}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac 2{\sin t }. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = -\sin t, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} = \cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} &= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac 1{\cos t} \cdot (-\sin t) + \dfrac 2{\sin t } \cdot \cos t \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac {\sin t}{\cos t} + 2 \cdot \dfrac {\cos t }{\sin t } \\[5pt] & = 2\cot{t} - \tan{t}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{2xy}}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2xy}} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{\ln t}{\sqrt{2t\ln t}} , \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{t}{\sqrt{2t\ln t}} . \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = 1, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac 1 t. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} & = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\ln t}{\sqrt{2t\ln t}} \cdot 1+ \dfrac{t}{\sqrt{2t\ln t}}\cdot \dfrac 1 t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\ln t}{\sqrt{2t\ln t}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2t\ln t}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1+\ln t}{\sqrt{2t\ln t}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = e^{xy} + xye^{xy}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = x^2e^{xy} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= e^{t^2\cdot t} + t^2\cdot te^{t^2\cdot t} = e^{t^3} + t^3e^{t^3} = (1+t^3)e^{t^3}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= (t^2)^2e^{t^2\cdot t} = t^4e^{t^3}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = 2t, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} = 1. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} &= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \\[5pt] &= (1+t^3)e^{t^3}\cdot 2t + t^4e^{t^3}\cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= (2t+2t^4)e^{t^3} + t^4e^{t^3} \\[5pt] &= (2t+3t^4)e^{t^3}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{2xy}{x^2+1}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \ln(x^2+1) \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{2x(x^2+1)}{x^2+1} = 2x, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= \ln(x^2+1). \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= 2x. \end{align*}

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} &= 2x + \ln(x^2+1)\cdot 2x \\[5pt] &= 2x(1 + \ln(x^2+1)). \end{align*}

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{y}{2\sqrt{xy-4}}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{xy-4}} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{x^2}{2\sqrt{x\cdot x^2-4}} =\dfrac{x^2}{2\sqrt{x^3-4}}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{x\cdot x^2-4}} =\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{x^3-4}}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= 2x. \end{align*}

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{x^2}{2\sqrt{x^3-4}} + \dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{x^3-4}}\cdot 2x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^2}{2\sqrt{x^3-4}} + \dfrac{2x^2}{2\sqrt{x^3-4}}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3x^2}{2\sqrt{x^3-4}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+x^6}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2(1+x^4)}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x}{x\sqrt{1+x^4}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^4}}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{x^3}{\sqrt{x^2+x^6}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^3}{\sqrt{x^2(1+x^4)}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^3}{x\sqrt{1 + x^4}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^4}}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= 3x^2. \end{align*}

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^4}} + \dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^4}} \cdot 3x^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^4}} + \dfrac{3x^4}{\sqrt{1+x^4}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1+3x^4}{\sqrt{1+x^4}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $f(x,y) = e^{x + y},$ where $x = s\sin{t}$ and $y = s\cos{t}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = e^{x + y}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = e^{x + y} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= e^{s\sin{t} + s\cos{t}}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= e^{s\sin{t} + s\cos{t}}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} &= s\cos{t}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} &= -s\sin{t}. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} & = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}\\[5pt] & = (e^{s\sin{t} + s\cos{t}})(s\cos{t}) + (e^{s\sin{t} + s\cos{t}})(-s\sin{t})\\[5pt] & = (s\cos{t} - s\sin{t})e^{s\sin{t} + s\cos{t}}\\[5pt] & = s(\cos{t} - \sin{t})e^{s(\sin{t} + \cos{t})}. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $f(x,y) = x - y,$ where $x = -s\cos{t}$ and $y = s\sin{t}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s}.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 1,\qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -1 \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= 1, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= -1. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} &= -\cos{t}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s} &= \sin{t}. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} & = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s}\\[5pt] & = (1)(-\cos{t}) + (-1)(\sin{t}) \\[5pt] & = -(\cos{t} + \sin{t}). \end{align*}

question.text: Let $f(x,y) = xy,$ where $x = \cos t + \sin s$ and $y = \sin t.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = x \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \sin t, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= \cos t + \sin s. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} &= -\sin t, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} &= \cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} & = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}\\[5pt] & = \sin t (-\sin t) + (\cos t + \sin s)\cdot \cos t\\[5pt] & = -\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t + \sin s \cos t. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $f(x,y) = xy^2 - 2y,$ where $x = st^2$ and $y = s^3 - t.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s}.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = y^2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2xy - 2 \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = (s^3 - t)^2 = s^6 - 2s^3t + t^2, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= 2(st^2)(s^3 - t) - 2 = 2s^4t^2 - 2st^3 - 2. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} &= t^2, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s} &= 3s^2. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} &= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s}\\[5pt] &= (s^6 - 2s^3t + t^2)(t^2) + (2s^4t^2 - 2st^3 - 2)(3s^2)\\[5pt] & = s^6 t^2 - 2s^3 t^3 + t^4 + 6s^6 t^2 - 6s^3 t^3 - 6s^2\\[5pt] & = 7s^6 t^2 - 8s^3 t^3 - 6s^2 + t^4. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $f(x,y) = \ln(x^2 + y^2),$ where $x = te^{s}$ and $y = te^{-s}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + y^2}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac{2y}{x^2 + y^2} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{2(te^{s})}{(te^{s})^2 + (te^{-s})^2} = \dfrac{2e^{s}}{t(e^{2s} + e^{-2s})}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{2(te^{-s})}{(te^{s})^2 + (te^{-s})^2} = \dfrac{2e^{-s}}{t(e^{2s} + e^{-2s})}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} &= e^{s}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} &= e^{-s}. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} & = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}\\[5pt] & =\dfrac{2e^{s}}{t(e^{2s} + e^{-2s})}\cdot e^{s} + \dfrac{2e^{-s}}{t(e^{2s} + e^{-2s})}\cdot e^{-s}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2e^{2s}}{t(e^{2s} + e^{-2s})} + \dfrac{2e^{-2s}}{t(e^{2s} + e^{-2s})}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2(e^{2s} + e^{-2s})}{t(e^{2s} + e^{-2s})}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2}{t}. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $f(x,y,z) = xy + yz + z^2,$ where $x = s^2 + t^2,$ $y = \dfrac{s}{t}$ and $z = st^2.$ Given that \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \dfrac{3s^2} t + c_1 t + c_2 st + c_3 st^4, \] find the value of $c_1 + c_2 + c_3.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t), y = y(s,t)$ and $z = z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial s} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x, y$ and $z\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = x + z, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} = y + 2z. \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{s}{t}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= s^2 + t^2 + st^2, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} &= \dfrac{s}{t} + 2st^2. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} &= 2s,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s} &= \dfrac{1}{t}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial s} &= t^2. \end{align*}

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} &= \left(\dfrac{s}{t}\right) \cdot 2s + (s^2 + t^2 + st^2) \cdot \dfrac{1}{t} + \left(\dfrac{s}{t} + 2st^2\right) \cdot t^2\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2s^2}{t} + \dfrac{s^2}{t} + t + st + st + 2st^4\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3s^2}{t} + t + 2st + 2st^4. \end{align*}

Finally, $c_1 = 1,$ $c_2 = 2$ and $c_3 = 2,$ and therefore \[ c_1 + c_2 + c_3 = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5. \]

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables

question.text: Let $f(x,y,z) = 3x - 2y + z,$ where $x = s+t,$ $y = s^2 - t^2$ and $z=s.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t), y = y(s,t)$ and $z = z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t}. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x, y$ and $z\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 3, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} = 1. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} &= 1, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} &= -2t, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t} &= 0. \end{align*}

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} & = (3)\cdot 1 + (-2)\cdot(-2t) + (1)\cdot 0\\[5pt] & = 4t + 3. \end{align*}

question.text:
Let $f(x,y,z) = x ^2+2xy-3z^2,$ where $x = st,$ $y = s+3t,$ and $z=2s - t.$ Given that \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = 2(s^2t + s^2 + c_1st + c_2s +c_3t), \]

find the value of $c_1+c_2+c_3.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t), y = y(s,t)$ and $z = z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t}. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x, y$ and $z\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2x+2y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2x, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} = -6z. \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= 2(st) + 2(s+3t) = 2st + 2s + 6t \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= 2st \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} &= -6(2s-t) = 6t-12s \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} &= s \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} &= 3 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t} &= -1 . \end{align*}

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} &= (2st + 2s + 6t)\cdot s + (2st)\cdot 3 + (6t-12s)\cdot (-1) \\[5pt] &= 2s^2t + 2s^2 + 6st + 6st - 6t + 12s \\[5pt] &= 2s^2t + 2s^2 + 12st + 12s - 6t\\[5pt] &=2(s^2t + s^2 + 6st + 6s - 3t) \end{align*}

Finally, $c_1 = c_2 = 6, c_3=-3,$ and therefore \[ c_1+c_2+c_3 = 6+6-3 = 9. \]

question.text: Let $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{y+z}{x},$ where $x = s+t,$ $y = s^2$ and $z=t^2 .$ Given that \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{c_1 s^2 + c_2 st + c_3 t^2}{(s+t)^2}, \] find the value of $c_1 + c_2 + c_3.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t), y = y(s,t)$ and $z = z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x, y$ and $z\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = -\dfrac{y+z}{x^2}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} = \dfrac{1}{x}. \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= -\dfrac{s^2 + t^2}{(s+t)^2},\\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{1}{s+t},\\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} &= \dfrac{1}{s+t}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} &= 1, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} &= 0, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t} &= 2t. \end{align*}

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} &= -\dfrac{s^2 + t^2}{(s+t)^2}\cdot (1) + \dfrac{1}{s+t}\cdot 0 + \dfrac{1}{s+t}\cdot 2t\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{-(s^2+t^2)+2t(s+t)}{(s+t)^2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{t^2+2ts-s^2}{(s+t)^2}. \end{align*}

Finally, $c_1 = -1,$ $c_2 = 2$ and $c_3 = 1,$ and therefore \[ c_1 + c_2 + c_3 = -1+2+1 = 2. \]

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables

question.text: Let $f(x,y,z) = xyz,$ where $x = 2,$ $y = se^{t}$ and $z=te^{s}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t), y = y(s,t)$ and $z = z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x, y$ and $z\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = yz, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = xz, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} = xy. \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= tse^{t+s}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= 2te^{s}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} &= 2se^{t}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} &= 0, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} &= se^{t}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t} &= e^{s}. \end{align*}

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} & = (tse^{t+s})\cdot 0 + (2te^{s})\cdot se^{t} + (2se^{t})\cdot e^{s}\\[5pt] & = 2tse^{t+ s} + 2se^{t+s}\\[5pt] & = 2s(t+1)e^{t+s}. \end{align*}
